en: We came to give.
We do not smoke,
Such is the problem
We will not return to the people on vacation.
It was bad for us
From the wind,
Our throat is broken,
People run, clap their hands,
There are many people standing
In the next war
Echen horse runner
Saddle stitch on the side
Many who once reveled now wander,
Many souls wander wailing,
And much livestock has been left ownerless.
“Alas, my dear brother,
He died innocently, for nothing,”
“On a road of torment with no turning back,
He met an infidel’s fate,”
Many people wander lamenting.
Yellow with wasting sickness,
Their hearts, minds, and thoughts
Are distracted—many among the people;
Yellow with wasting sickness,
Many mortals suffer anxiety,
And all their reason and thoughts
Are distracted as well;
Some have perished in battle,
And others too have died.
“Ah, Sarybai, we are done for,” they say,
“Through Choro, the blue-maned brother,
We have endured great calamity,” they say.
“I shall seize the lands
Of the consummate blue-maned lions,” he said,
“I, brother to a lion, a bloodthirsty tyrant,
Shall oppress the people,” he said.
“An army from the whole world gathered,
But in the end we were miserably slaughtered;
He slew so many of us,” they say.
“He heeds no guilt or pity,
But wrought a total massacre,” they say.
Their cruppers torn apart,
Many wander ruined among the host;
Their girths snapped,
Their saddles slipped beneath their bellies,
Many people rush about in panic.
Staggering senseless in confusion,
Their two legs dangling,
Every knee scraped raw,
Every rein torn apart,
Armor ripped and fluttering,
Spears shattered with a shriek,
“Ah, Sarybai has slain us,” they say,
“He killed until his fury was spent,” they say.
“The people are ruined in massacre;
Thus has God struck us,” they say.
“This tyrant’s offspring
Would humiliate and slaughter us,” they say.
“This monstrous slave Sarybai
Has made sport of countless men,” they say.
“The Lord Creator made Sarybai
Great and powerful,” they say.
“He inflicted misery and humiliation;
Sarybai is a vicious dog,
He has butchered us all,” they say.
“If death should overtake us suddenly,
If by mischance we perish,
We shall know him for the dog he is,
If the rumors told are true.
On the Judgment Morning at dawn,
That swaggering swine
We shall make ride a black donkey,” they said.
So the army clamored,
Until the host lost its senses,
And while they poured out their grief,
Kulansur, the steed he rode,
Flew rumbling like a cloud;
The stones struck by his hooves
Shattered with a ringing cry.
Rearing and surging forward,
The riderless Kulansur
Shot ahead like an arrow;
That splendid steed had a flowing mane,
And for the young hero Seytek
He had been born a perfect match.
When he glided, he was like a snake;
When he wheeled, he was like a whirlwind;
When he strode, he was like a wild ass—
Such was the nature of that horse.
The riderless fleet-footed steed
He made rear and plunge,
And seized the white reins knotted in a loop.
The reins fitted Kulansur perfectly;
He gripped them hard in both hands,
And wrestled with the mouth
Of the black steed flying like a cloud.
The reins stretched thin as thread;
When the black steed saw the mountain
And bucked, the black earth
Was gouged out on every side.
When he struck out with unerring steps,
The ground he trod burst apart;
A cloud of dust as large as a house
Whirled above the head
Of the fortunate hero.
His broad front teeth, like a gate,
Shone like steel within his mouth;
The black steed’s splayed stride
Appeared as broad as a ravine.
The polished steel spear in his hand
Danced and darted in his grasp;
The descendant of the noble lion
Wore the aspect of one thirsting for blood.
Those he charged were scorched to ashes;
Those he struck ceased to exist.
He reached the army and cut through it,
Spearing everyone he met.
He swung the spear in his hand,
Aimed it at the hollow
Above each breastbone, and drove it home.
The axe flashed in his hand,
The iron mace crashed upon heads;
Blood poured from those he struck,
Life fled from those he smote.
His spear blazed like a fiery ember,
And no one struck by it remained.
Sarybai, who had advanced in force,
Halted as though he had drunk poison.
Every rein was cut,
And the vast host he had summoned
Was now gathered
Before Sarybai.
The people lost their senses,
The vast army rose in uproar,
Pressing around Sarybai;
Many commanders of the host
Gathered around Sarybai,
And the people assembled with a clamor.
The great army that had gone to war
Despaired of its precious life.
His matchless lionhearted courage,
His valor famed through the ages,
Revealed the hero Seytek;
Wherever he carved into them, they split apart.
He did not merely raise a furious clash—
Every soul despaired.
“My wrestlers, my lions,” he cried,
Toppling them backward from their horses,
He defeated and drove them onward.
The spear he thrust seemed to lengthen,
His eyes reddened like a lion’s;
Breaking the ranks of the countless host,
He swallowed them up and drove them on.
“May his forefather Manas stand beside him,” they said,
“May God set every deed aright,” they said.
He roared in fury,
Slaughtering, driving, and scattering them;
The world filled with dust,
And their heads reeled in bewilderment.
He speared them one after another,
Crushing the ground wherever he passed;
The side he advanced upon became deserted,
Those he faced were consumed by fire,
And all he encountered were slain.
He made Kulansur dance,
And made everyone he met cry out;
In groups of a hundred and forty
He herded them away.
He bent the brave double,
Slaughtering as he went.
Those who resisted and stood their ground,
Those who swaggered like men
And faced him defiantly,
Along with their comrades—
Thirty tigers who had closed around them,
A fold no wind could penetrate,
And thirty-five companions—
He left their arms hanging limp,
And, without killing them, left their eyes staring;
Tormenting them while still alive,
He bound them and drove them away.
Those wretches who would not submit
He prodded with his spear
And drove away.
At the sight, the heart was overwhelmed;
They loomed like a blue hill,
The lions Manas and Semetey
Appeared like a deep blue valley.
They wounded all who took up spears,
Cutting through the sixfold host;
When within reach, they speared them,
And those who came close enough to strike
They smashed with battle-axes.
Those they faced they stretched out dead,
Those they met they felled;
Those who came face-to-face
They destroyed with swords,
And those who ventured even closer
They struck down with battle-axes.
The earth turned green-black, filled with blood;
For the return of peaceful, joyous times
The vast army yearned.
The people cried out in uproar,
Fleeing ridge to ridge for shelter;
Hero Külchoro and hero Seytek
Moved among the people like tigers.
Those fated to live escaped by cunning,
Those doomed to die could not escape.
Hero Seytek hewed through their center
To right and left,
While through their very midst went Külchoro
Upon his red-roan horse—
A blooded courser that had witnessed much,
Its champion rider a master of the spear,
A man seasoned from his youth,
Who had seen the turmoil of combat
From the age of twelve.
Your capable elder Külchoro
Drove Sarybai’s vast army
Ahead of him,
While hero Seytek
Struck down their warriors.
The people gathered with cries;
What vast turmoil and mighty conflict!
They attacked and were themselves destroyed.
Delighting in Zhelpinish,
The ogre’s son, deeming himself a hero,
Reaped men down as if at play.
“You have stirred up boundless strife,” they said;
“He who attacks first must not weep—
Go now to your God,” they said.
He swung and thrust his polished spear,
Breaking apart the ranks
Of that turbulent, ruinous conflict.
The hapless people were needlessly trapped;
The ogre’s son was ruined.
All the heroes assembled,
Wrestlers and giants were slain;
Their vision dimmed and clouded,
The warriors’ path was blocked.
Such was the state of the battle:
They began the shooting and slaughter,
And when the two lions
Fought beneath the moon,
The two of them utterly renounced
Their lives held only in trust.
The consummate warriors, the noble lions,
Speared everyone who came,
Crushing six thousand.
Hero Sarybai, of great fame and terrible might,
Kept pressing onward,
Crushing everyone he encountered,
Spearing all who resisted.
Ah, the arrogant dog kept pressing on.
All the warriors burned with grief,
Each hero despaired of his life;
